<reason>Side A won every major clash by grounding its case in the actual legal and economic mechanics of college athletics. Side A established that public universities are governed by state labor laws—many of which outlaw public-sector collective bargaining—making uniform conference-wide bargaining legally impossible without sweeping legislative overhauls that Side B was forced to concede in Rebuttal 2. Side A also cleanly dismantled Side B's cross-subsidization arguments by distinguishing external booster NIL funds from internal institutional revenue, pointing out that Title IX binds schools rather than unions, and exposing the flaw in comparing multi-sport college athletics to the single-sport, roster-capped NFLPA. Finally, Side A directly answered Side B's pressure questions by explaining why mandatory union wage floors—rather than tiered revenue sharing itself—force roster cuts.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In Rebuttal 2 [A4.4-A4.5], Side A dismantled Side B's Pressure Question answers by showing that relying on "federal preemption or state reform" conceded that collective bargaining is currently illegal at many public flagships, and by exposing why the NFLPA—which represents a single revenue sport with strict roster caps and faces no Title IX mandate—cannot prove that football players would voluntarily subsidize Olympic sports.</best_rebuttal>
